rows.label: Industrial production
rows.note: Cyclical and volatile; turns before the labour market.

rows.label: IP: final products
rows.note: The demand end of the production chain.

rows.label: IP: consumer goods
rows.note: Separates household demand from business demand inside IP.

rows.label: IP: business equipment
rows.note: Capex in volume terms, and the most cyclical slice of IP.

rows.label: IP: materials
rows.note: Upstream of the other three, so it turns first in a goods cycle.

rows.label: Capacity utilization
rows.note: A utilisation rate, so differenced. The slack measure the Taylor rule work leans on.

rows.label: Real GDP
rows.note: The definition of output, four months late. Enters as a quarterly block so the Mariano-Murasawa aggregation ties it to three latent monthly values instead of pretending it is a monthly series with gaps.

rows.label: IP: manufacturing
rows.note: Manufacturing on the SIC basis, the longest-running cut.

rows.label: Durable goods orders
rows.note: Orders lead shipments lead production. Noisy: aircraft alone can move the headline several percent.

rows.label: Core capital goods orders
rows.note: Non-defence capital goods ex aircraft — the same signal with the two worst sources of noise removed.

rows.label: Unfilled orders: durables
rows.note: The backlog. Falling unfilled orders with flat shipments is production running ahead of demand.

rows.label: Business inventories
rows.note: Slow, and worth the wait: inventory is where a demand miss shows up before anyone admits it.

rows.label: Inventory/sales ratio
rows.note: A ratio, so differenced. Rising means stock accumulating against sales, which is the recession tell.

rows.label: Nonfarm payrolls
rows.note: The fastest broad read, and the one the rest wait for.

rows.label: Unemployment rate
rows.note: A rate, so differenced rather than log-differenced.

rows.label: U-6 underemployment
rows.note: Includes part-time-for-economic-reasons, so it deteriorates before the headline rate does.

rows.label: Labor force participation
rows.note: The denominator. A falling unemployment rate on falling participation is not a tightening labour market.

rows.label: Mfg weekly hours
rows.note: Hours move before heads; already stationary in level.

rows.label: Mfg overtime hours
rows.note: The first margin an employer cuts, ahead of hours and heads.

rows.label: Manufacturing employment
rows.note: The cyclical end of the labor market.

rows.label: Construction employment
rows.note: The rate-sensitive end, and the fastest read on housing.

rows.label: Retail trade employment
rows.note: Hiring against expected consumption, not realised.

rows.label: Service-providing employment
rows.note: Five sixths of jobs. Slow to turn, which is the point: it confirms rather than leads.

rows.label: Initial claims
rows.note: The highest-frequency labour read there is, five days behind. Weekly, so collapsed to a monthly observation.

rows.label: Continuing claims
rows.note: Initial claims say who lost a job; continuing claims say whether they found another.

rows.label: JOLTS job openings
rows.note: Labour demand rather than labour outcomes. Slow, and the numerator of the vacancy-to-unemployed ratio.

rows.label: JOLTS quits rate
rows.note: A rate, so differenced. Quits are a worker-confidence read and they lead wage growth.

rows.label: JOLTS layoffs rate
rows.note: The other side of quits. Layoffs rising while quits fall is the labour market breaking, not cooling.

rows.label: Mean duration unemployed
rows.note: Lengthening duration is how a soft landing turns hard.

rows.label: Real retail sales
rows.note: Consumption in volume terms, so inflation does not leak in.

rows.label: Real consumption
rows.note: Two thirds of output, three weeks behind payrolls.

rows.label: Real disposable income
rows.note: What funds consumption; turns earlier in an income shock.

rows.label: Real income ex transfers
rows.note: Strips out government payments, so it reads earned income only — the cut the NBER dating committee watches.

rows.label: Personal saving rate
rows.note: A rate, so differenced. Consumption held up by a falling saving rate is borrowed from next quarter.

rows.label: U Michigan sentiment
rows.note: A survey, so a level index rather than a quantity. Fast, and the soft-data counterweight to the hard series above.

rows.label: Total vehicle sales
rows.note: The big-ticket, credit-financed end of consumption — where a rate shock lands first.

rows.label: Housing starts
rows.note: Rate-sensitive and early. Logged, not differenced — the level of log starts is the cycle.

rows.label: Building permits
rows.note: One step ahead of starts, and less weather-sensitive.

rows.label: Housing starts: Northeast
rows.note: The regional cuts are kept because the national figure is thin enough that one region's weather can carry it.

rows.label: Housing starts: Midwest
rows.note: See HOUSTNE.

rows.label: Housing starts: South
rows.note: Roughly half of national starts, so it dominates the aggregate — worth watching on its own.

rows.label: Housing starts: West
rows.note: The most rate-sensitive region by price level.

rows.label: New one-family houses sold
rows.note: Sales against the starts above; the gap is builder inventory.

rows.label: Case-Shiller national HPI
rows.note: A price index, so a second log difference. Three months late and a three-month moving average on top — slow by design.

rows.label: 30y mortgage rate
rows.note: The transmission channel from policy to housing, same-day weekly. Differenced; the level is not stationary.

rows.label: CPI
rows.note: Price indices take a second log difference: the first gives inflation, the second gives whether inflation is turning.

rows.label: Core CPI
rows.note: Ex food and energy; less noisy, slower to turn.

rows.label: CPI energy
rows.note: The volatile component the core strips out, kept separately so an energy shock is identifiable rather than absorbed.

rows.label: CPI food
rows.note: The other stripped component, and the one households feel.

rows.label: CPI commodities
rows.note: Goods prices. Tradeable, so this is where the dollar and tariffs show up.

rows.label: CPI services
rows.note: Non-tradeable and wage-driven, so it is the persistent half. The goods/services split is the whole 2021-2024 argument.

rows.label: PCE price index
rows.note: The Fed's actual target, two weeks behind CPI.

rows.label: Core PCE
rows.note: The specific number the FOMC statement refers to.

rows.label: PPI all commodities
rows.note: Upstream, so it leads consumer prices on a cost shock.

rows.label: PPI final demand
rows.note: The current headline PPI concept; PPIACO is the long history.

rows.label: PPI finished consumer goods
rows.note: The slice of PPI that maps most directly onto CPI goods.

rows.label: Average hourly earnings
rows.note: The wage side of inflation, and the fastest price read.

rows.label: Employment cost index: wages
rows.note: Slower than average hourly earnings and far cleaner: the ECI holds job mix fixed, so it does not move when the composition of employment shifts. Quarterly.

rows.label: M1 money stock
rows.note: Narrow money. The 2020 definitional change makes the level incomparable across that break; the second difference of logs is what survives it.

rows.label: M2 money stock
rows.note: Broad money, and the aggregate the 2021 inflation argument was actually conducted in.

rows.label: Real M2
rows.note: M2 deflated by CPI — purchasing power rather than nominal stock, so one log difference, not two.

rows.label: Monetary base
rows.note: Central bank money specifically, as distinct from deposits.

rows.label: Total reserves
rows.note: Bank reserves at the Fed — the quantity balance-sheet policy operates on directly.

rows.label: Fed balance sheet
rows.note: Total assets, weekly, one day behind. The quantitative side of policy, which the funds rate does not capture.

rows.label: Treasury general account
rows.note: A level in billions, already stationary enough to use raw. Moves reserves around without any policy decision, which is why it belongs next to WALCL rather than inside an interpretation of it.

rows.label: Overnight reverse repo
rows.note: The Fed's daily repo facility take-up, published same day. The drain that stood between the balance sheet and reserves through 2022-2024. One of ~2,000 observations was corrected between the 2023 snapshot and today, by $0.103bn against a series that routinely moves by hundreds of billions.

rows.label: Total consumer credit
rows.note: Household borrowing. Slow — a G.19 release is two months out.

rows.label: Revolving consumer credit
rows.note: Card balances. Rising revolving credit against flat income is consumption being financed rather than earned.

rows.label: Nonrevolving consumer credit
rows.note: Auto and student loans — a different decision from a card balance, so kept separate.

rows.label: Commercial & industrial loans
rows.note: Bank credit to firms, from the weekly H.8 aggregated monthly.

rows.label: Real estate loans
rows.note: The largest bank asset class, and the one a CRE shock hits.

rows.label: Total C&I loans (weekly)
rows.note: The same concept as BUSLOANS at weekly frequency, nine days behind instead of six weeks. Both are kept: the monthly one has the history, the weekly one has the edge.

rows.label: Loan officer survey: tightening
rows.note: A net-percentage diffusion index, already bounded, so it enters in level. The only direct read on credit SUPPLY rather than credit outstanding — quantities cannot distinguish nobody wanting to borrow from nobody being allowed to. Quarterly.

rows.label: High yield OAS
rows.note: A spread in percent, so level. FRED's ICE BofA licence exposes only a rolling window — roughly three years of history, which is why this cannot anchor a long backtest and is present for the current-state read.

rows.label: Baa - 10y spread
rows.note: Moody's Baa over the 10y Treasury, daily back to 1986. The long credit-stress history the ICE series lacks.

rows.label: Aaa - 10y spread
rows.note: The investment-grade end. Baa-minus-Aaa is the part of the spread that is default risk rather than duration.

rows.label: Chicago Fed financial conditions
rows.note: The broadest financial-conditions composite there is — 105 indicators of risk, credit and leverage on one zero-centred scale, so level. Two separate limits, measured: FRED 504s on the archive request from 1980, which the 2005 start works around, and the archive ITSELF only begins 2011-05-27 whatever start is asked for. The revised series goes back to 1971 and is deliberately not used.

rows.label: Adjusted NFCI
rows.note: NFCI with the part explained by the real economy and inflation projected out, so what is left is financial conditions that are NOT just the cycle. The pair is the decomposition; neither half is the other's substitute.

rows.label: St Louis financial stress
rows.note: A composite index centred on zero, so level. The vintage archive only starts in 2022 because the index was rebuilt; point-in-time depth is short.

rows.label: Fed funds effective
rows.note: The policy rate itself, differenced. The monthly average, which is the series the Taylor rule work is calibrated on.

rows.label: 2y Treasury
rows.note: The maturity that prices the expected policy path. Differenced; a yield level is not stationary.

rows.label: 10y Treasury
rows.note: The discount rate for everything else.

rows.label: 10y-2y slope
rows.note: A spread, so level. Already the difference of two non-stationary yields.

rows.label: 10y-3m slope
rows.note: The slope with the better recession record of the two, because the front end is the policy rate rather than an expectation of it.

rows.label: 10y breakeven
rows.note: Market-implied inflation compensation. Not an expectation — it carries a risk premium — but it is the daily one, against surveys that are monthly at best.

rows.label: 10y TIPS real yield
rows.note: The real rate. Nominal minus breakeven by construction, and the channel a policy surprise travels down.

rows.label: VIX
rows.note: Implied volatility in points, so level. The regime work found volatility, not means, is where monthly macro regime structure actually lives. Not perfectly unrevised: 2 of 2,020 observations moved between the 2023 snapshot and today, by at most 0.08 vol points — two corrections in eight years, three orders of magnitude below the series' own daily range. Stated rather than rounded to never.

rows.label: Broad dollar index
rows.note: Trade-weighted, so it is the dollar that matters for import prices rather than one cross. Reads the ARCHIVE, not the current series, and that is a measured correction rather than caution: the two disagree on 91% of overlapping days by up to 2.18 index points, because the H.10 basket weights are re-estimated annually and applied backwards. A constructed index is not a quote. Costs history — the archive starts 2019-02 — and is worth it. See artifacts/reports/macro_route_verification.json.

rows.label: S&P 500
rows.note: FRED serves a rolling ten-year window, so this cannot carry a long backtest. The same licence makes the route UNVERIFIABLE: both the archive and the as-of snapshot return 400, so unlike the other members of this route the no-revisions claim here is reasoning about an index close, not a measurement. Flagged rather than filed with the ones that were checked.

rows.label: Nonfarm payrolls
rows.note: The fastest broad read on the economy, and the one the rest wait for.

rows.label: Industrial production
rows.note: Cyclical and volatile; turns before the labour market.

rows.label: Real retail sales
rows.note: Consumption in volume terms, so inflation does not leak into growth.

rows.label: Real consumption
rows.note: Two thirds of output, but it publishes three weeks behind payrolls.

rows.label: Real disposable income
rows.note: What funds the consumption above; turns earlier in an income shock.

rows.label: CPI
rows.note: Headline. What households and index-linked contracts actually face.

rows.label: Core CPI
rows.note: Ex food and energy; less noisy, and slower to turn.

rows.label: Producer prices
rows.note: Upstream, so it leads consumer prices when the shock is a cost shock.
